entry.title: Chulapa v2.2.0: more ways to make your site yours

link.title: Chulapa v2.2.0: more ways to make your site yours

entry.content:
Dark mode, diagrams, galleries and new starter examples

2 min.

Chulapa v2.2.0 is out.

This release adds a few features that I have wanted to bring to the theme for some time: a light/dark skin selector, Mermaid diagrams, PhotoSwipe galleries and complete starter examples. There are also several smaller changes around navigation, accessibility and the bundled skins.

Here is a quick overview of what is new.

Light and dark skins

Chulapa can now let visitors choose between light, dark and automatic appearances.

You just need to configure a second skin. The theme then adds a selector to the classic, floating and dual navigation bars. The selected appearance is remembered across pages and tabs and, importantly, it is applied before the page is displayed.

This is completely opt-in. If you do not configure a dark skin, your site works as before and no additional styles or scripts for the selector are loaded.

See how to configure light and dark skins.

Mermaid diagrams

Another addition in v2.2.0 is support for Mermaid diagrams.

Mermaid can be enabled per page, so the library is only loaded when it is actually needed. Once enabled, diagrams can be added using fenced blocks directly in your Markdown content.

There is also a fallback: if Mermaid cannot render a diagram, the original source remains available.

The Mermaid guide has all the details.

PhotoSwipe galleries

Masonry galleries and carousels can now use PhotoSwipe to provide a zoomable image viewer.

PhotoSwipe is optional and supports keyboard and touch controls, reduced-motion preferences and the original image link as a fallback.

You can see how to enable PhotoSwipe or check the live demo.

GoatCounter analytics

v2.2.0 also adds support for GoatCounter as a lightweight analytics option.

It is disabled by default and, when configured, the script is loaded asynchronously only in production builds.

See the GoatCounter setup guide for the configuration details.

Navigation and new skins

There are a few other visible changes.

Tables of contents now highlight the section currently being viewed. This is particularly useful on longer documentation pages and posts.

The release also adds three new skins: Cerulean, Litera and Pulse. I have also reviewed text contrast across many components of the bundled skins. Some upstream color combinations still fall below the WCAG 4.5:1 contrast benchmark, so it is worth checking the result if you use one of these skins or custom colors.

You can compare all of them in the skin previews.

Starter examples

One thing that was missing from the documentation was a simple way to see how a complete Chulapa site fits together.

v2.2.0 adds four starter examples:

  • personal blog
  • technical blog
  • portfolio
  • project site

Each example includes the configuration and content files needed to reproduce the site, together with a working demo.

See the starter examples or browse the demos.

Updating to v2.2.0

For sites using the remote theme, update _config.yml:

remote_theme: dieghernan/chulapa@v2.2.0

For gem-based installations, update the version in your Gemfile:

gem "chulapa-jekyll", "~> 2.2.0"

and run:

bundle update chulapa-jekyll

The installation guide covers both methods.

If you are upgrading an existing site, especially one with local overrides of layouts or includes, I recommend previewing it locally before publishing.

The full release notes have the complete list of changes.

As always, issues, suggestions and examples of sites built with Chulapa are welcome in GitHub Discussions.
entry.summary: Chulapa v2.2.0 is out, with support for light and dark skins, Mermaid diagrams, PhotoSwipe galleries, new starter examples and several improvements across the theme.

entry.title: Chulapa v2.1.0: more control over your site

link.title: Chulapa v2.1.0: more control over your site

entry.content:
New looks, more search options and better metadata

5 min.

Chulapa v2.1.0 is here. This release gives you more control over how your site looks, how readers find its content and how pages appear when shared.

When I first built Chulapa, I wanted a theme I could use for different sites while giving each one its own look. The idea is still the same. You can choose a skin, change a few settings in _config.yml and make the site your own. This release adds more ways to do that, along with some useful fixes behind the scenes.

Here are the changes I would start exploring.

Give each page the right introduction

A page title has several jobs. It introduces the content on the page, appears in the browser tab and helps describe a link when someone shares it. You may want different wording for each of those places.

In v2.1.0, seo_title and og_title let you set the metadata titles separately from the visible heading. The new description option also gives you an explicit metadata description, independent of the subtitle and excerpt:

---
layout: default
title: "My field notes"
subtitle: "A weekend exploring the mountains"
seo_title: "Mountain field notes | My travel blog"
og_title: "A weekend in the mountains"
description: "Routes, observations and practical notes from a mountain weekend."
---

The theme shares that description across HTML, Open Graph, Twitter/X cards and JSON-LD, without forcing it into a fixed character limit. You can keep the introduction on the page conversational and write a separate description for people encountering its link elsewhere.

There is more control over the rest of the metadata, too. canonical_url provides a consistent preferred URL across the page’s metadata, breadcrumbs and feeds. Page language and Open Graph locales can be configured separately, and translated locales can be listed. Article metadata includes publication and modification dates, authors, sections and tags where supplied.

For sites with several contributors, the JSON-LD publisher can now be configured independently of the author. Sharing images can have explicit alternative text, dimensions and a MIME type, while schema_image identifies representative article images for structured data.

These settings help describe your content accurately. They do not guarantee a particular search result or social preview, so check a few real pages after updating. The metadata reference and global settings explain the options and their defaults.

One theme, more looks

This release adds 13 skins, including listen, navi, cyborg, darkly, slate, solar and the butterfly variants. There are also more code highlighting styles, including github.dark, nord, one.dark and stackoverflow.light.

The configuration stays familiar. For example, to combine the Navi skin with Nord code highlighting:

chulapa-skin:
  skin: navi
  highlight: nord

Browse the skin previews and syntax highlighting examples to compare them with your own content. Skin names are case-sensitive: use the filename without its .scss extension.

Titles and subtitles now support Markdown as well as HTML. A little emphasis or an inline code name can be written using the same syntax as the rest of your post.

Give readers another way to find your content

Chulapa now supports Fuse.js and Simple-Jekyll-Search, alongside the existing search providers. Both use an index generated during the Jekyll build, so they are useful options for a static site.

To select Fuse.js in _config.yml:

search:
  provider: fusejs
  maxwords: 30

Use provider: simplesearch to select Simple-Jekyll-Search. The maxwords setting controls how much page content is included in these indexes; it is not a limit on the number of results. Pages can be excluded with include_on_search: false.

The provider needs a separate page using layout: search, with a permalink matching search.landing_page (by default, /search). Changing the provider does not create that page for you.

Fuse.js and Lunr results now highlight matching terms, helping readers see why a page appeared. When updating an older Lunr configuration, replace search.lunr_maxwords with search.maxwords. The old option still works and takes precedence if both are present, so remove it when migrating.

See the search configuration for provider-specific settings and setup.

Make room for different kinds of pages

The minimal layout is useful when you want to control your own content width and structure. In v2.1.0, it can also reuse a theme header:

---
layout: minimal
title: "A project of my own"
show_header: true
header_type: base
---

The header is optional, and the layout stays headerless by default. Enabling it does not add a content container: your markup still controls the page’s width and spacing. Try the minimal header demo for an example.

At the end of an article, show_random adds another way to discover content, and related_label and random_label let you customize the introductions to those cards. Random selection happens at build time, using the same tag-based candidate pool as related content; it does not select a new set on each visit.

The layouts reference covers those options and the other components you can enable on a page.

A few important fixes behind the scenes

Some of the most useful changes are the ones you should barely notice. Canonical URLs, breadcrumbs and feeds now preserve filenames containing index.html. Metadata avoids repeated subtitles and empty title separators, and guest pages no longer inherit the site author’s Twitter/X attribution.

Video structured data now uses the correct URLs before and after deferred playback. Video snippets also accept optional titles, thumbnails, dates, descriptions and durations. The main theme script and deferred video player load from the installed theme, and minimal pages without a maincontent element no longer trigger the previous JavaScript error.

Font Awesome’s fa_kit_code setting now loads the configured kit. If you still have fa5_kit_code, it remains supported and takes precedence when both keys are present. Check that combination if a kit change seems to have no effect.

You can find the full list, including the new skins and highlighting styles, in the v2.1.0 release notes.

Try v2.1.0 on your site

For a remote-theme installation, pin the release in _config.yml:

remote_theme: dieghernan/chulapa@v2.1.0

For a gem-based installation, set the version constraint in your Gemfile:

gem "chulapa-jekyll", "~> 2.1.0"

Then run bundle update chulapa-jekyll and rebuild your site. Version 2.1.0 is available on RubyGems. The installation guide covers the required plugins and deployment steps for each method.

Preview a post, a standalone page and your search results before deploying. If you use custom layouts or includes, check them alongside the theme’s examples. For metadata changes, inspect the generated titles, descriptions and canonical URLs on a few representative pages.

The release was checked with Jekyll 3.10.0 and 4.4.1. That is useful coverage, but your own content, plugins and overrides still deserve a preview.

A sneak peek at what’s next

There is already more work on the development branch: optional Mermaid diagrams for technical content, keyboard navigation and visible-focus improvements, and four small starter examples for blogs, portfolios and project pages.

These changes are not part of v2.1.0. They are a preview of the next stage, with no release date promised here. If you try the development branch, keep its version caveats in mind; the pinned release above gives you v2.1.0.

If you give Chulapa a go, I would love to see what you build. Share your site or feedback in GitHub Discussions.
entry.summary: Explore Chulapa v2.1.0, from page metadata and new skins to search and layout options, with a small preview of what comes next.

entry.title: Ask Chulapa
entry.content:
A new way to explore the documentation

1 min.

The Chulapa documentation now has an AI assistant . You can open it from the AI button on the homepage or documentation pages and ask about installation, skins, configuration, layouts and other documented features.

Try a specific question such as “How do I change my site’s skin?” or “How do I add a local video?” The assistant can provide short explanations, code examples and links to the relevant documentation. Each question is independent, so include the details it needs rather than relying on an earlier message.

Recent messages and the draft stay in the current tab’s sessionStorage so reloading a page can restore the interface. Clear chat resets those messages and the draft. This displayed history is not sent as conversation context: each request contains only the current question.

Following a link from the assistant in the same tab closes its panel so you can read the destination. Reopening it restores your messages and draft. Opening a link in a new tab leaves the original panel open.

The assistant uses Cloudflare Workers AI with a reviewed summary of the docs. Questions are sent to Cloudflare for processing. Answers can contain mistakes; check the linked documentation, especially before changing your configuration. Site search remains available when you want to explore the original pages.

This is an addition to the documentation site. It is not bundled with the reusable theme and does not require an AI account to use Chulapa on your own site.

I wrote a more personal account of the development, including context selection, answer testing and the mobile interface, on my blog: Building a documentation chatbot for Chulapa.
entry.summary: Ask questions about Chulapa and get practical examples with links to the docs.

entry.title: Welcome
entry.content:
1 min.

Welcome to Chulapa. This is another Jekyll theme that you can use for creating your site.

Motivation

In the last couple of years I created some tiny websites using GitHub Pages. However, I was not very happy with some of the thousands of Jekyll themes available, since I didn’t find one that met all my requirements:

  • Easy to use
  • Awesome looking
  • Plenty of add-ons
  • Feed

So, as a way to challenge myself, I decided to build this one from scratch. My main references were Beautiful Jekyll and Minimal Mistakes, that are two pretty good options, much more mature than this one and with hundreds of users. So, why not learn from them? There are pieces and components of these themes on this one.

One theme, a thousand looks

Without prior knowledge of CSS, I taught myself about rules, specificities, flexboxes, etc. through implementing Bootstrap v4 as the CSS base of Chulapa.

This is not the first theme with this implementation, but I found the way to configure it via _config.yml, which allows any user to easily change the look of the site without needing to write CSS or SCSS. On top of that, implementing Bootstrap themes from third parties is fast and reliable.

The huge advantage is that, if you give it a go, you can use Chulapa in any site you want but still define a unique look to each of them. No one could notice that the theme is the same!

Next steps

When this post was written in May 2020, Chulapa was still in development. Stable releases are now available; see the installation guide for setup instructions.

The theme currently uses Bootstrap 4 and Font Awesome 6, with support for Font Awesome 5 and optional v4 shims. See the changelog for subsequent changes.
entry.summary: Welcome to Chulapa. This is another Jekyll theme that you can use for creating your site.
